html:
In July 2000 the Taliban leader Mullah Omar banned the growing of opium poppies in Afghanistan, then the source of most of the world's illegal opium and heroin.

The ban was strictly enforced. In 2001 the poppy harvest in Taliban areas almost vanished, one of the most effective drug bans ever seen. The Taliban said it was a religious duty; many observers thought they also wanted international recognition and aid, and some noted that stocks of stored opium rose in value. Farmers who depended on the crop fell deep into debt and hunger.

The ban did not last. After the Taliban fell in late 2001, poppy fields spread again, above all in Helmand, and through the 2000s Afghanistan supplied around 90 percent of the world's illegal opium. When the Taliban returned to power they banned opium again in 2022, again with sharp results.
sum: In July 2000 the Taliban leader Mullah Omar banned the growing of opium poppies in Afghanistan, then the source of most of the world's illegal opium and heroin.
